passage:
Below a steep icefall the surface of a glacier is often marked by a series of bands that curve downstream, one pair of them for each year the ice has travelled. A light band and a dark band together record a single annual cycle. The dark band is ice that crossed the icefall in summer: the broken surface exposed there is large, melting is rapid, and wind-blown dust settles on ice that is wasting rather than gathering. Ice that crossed the same ground in winter emerges relatively clean and, being thicker, stands slightly higher.

The bands are therefore a record of what happened at one place, the foot of the icefall, and not of conditions along the glacier as a whole. Their spacing is the distance the ice travels in a year, so a narrowing of successive bands downstream is read as a slowing of the flow rather than as a change in the weather.
prompt: [Academic — Glaciology] What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Paired bands at the foot of an icefall record one year of travel and can be read for the rate of the flow.
Dust carried onto a glacier by the wind is the main control on how quickly its surface wastes away.
A glacier below an icefall loses more ice in summer than in winter, and the difference can be seen from the surface.
Marks on the surface of a glacier are a better guide to past weather than the thickness of the ice beneath them.
correct_answer: Paired bands at the foot of an icefall record one year of travel and can be read for the rate of the flow.
explanation: The passage derives the pair of bands from one annual cycle and closes by using their spacing to read the speed of the ice, which is the option about one year of travel and the rate of the flow. The option about dust makes one ingredient of the dark band into the whole subject; the option about summer and winter loss stops at a seasonal contrast the passage uses only as a step; and the option comparing surface marks with ice thickness draws a comparison the passage never makes, and the last sentence refuses the weather reading outright.

passage:
A pendulum clock keeps time by the length of its pendulum, and metal lengthens as it warms. A rod that grows by a fraction of a millimetre over a summer will lose several seconds a day, and for the first seventy years of the pendulum clock this was the limit on what it could do.

John Harrison's answer was to build the pendulum from two metals that expand by different amounts. Brass and steel rods were fixed alternately in a frame, so that the brass, which expands the more of the two, pushed the bob upward by as much as the lengthening steel let it fall. What mattered was not the length of any one rod but the difference between the two sets, and that could be adjusted by cutting a rod shorter. The device compensated for temperature and for nothing else. Changes in air pressure, which alter the buoyancy of the bob, were left for later makers to deal with.
prompt: [Academic — Horology] According to the passage, the brass rods in the frame
choices: lift the bob by as much as the steel rods let it drop
lengthen less in warm weather than steel rods of the same size

take the weight of the bob so that the steel is not put under strain
correct_answer: lift the bob by as much as the steel rods let it drop
explanation: The passage has the brass pushing the bob upward by as much as the lengthening steel lets it fall, which is the option about lifting the bob by as much as the steel lets it drop. Brass is said to expand the more of the two, not the less; cutting a rod shorter is offered as a way of adjusting the difference between the sets and not as a way of matching their weights; and the load carried by either metal is never discussed.

passage:
The green of a celadon glaze comes from iron, and the same iron will give a yellow or a brown. Which colour appears depends less on the recipe than on the air in the kiln during the firing. Where the fire is given plenty of air the iron takes up oxygen and settles in its ferric form, which is yellow-brown. Where the flue is damped down and the fire burns with too little air, the flames draw oxygen from whatever will yield it, the iron in the glaze included, and the ferrous form that results is green.

A potter therefore governed colour by governing a draught, and a single kiln load could come out unevenly because one corner drew better than another. Pieces from one firing are still sorted by tone. The wares that were kept were not the ones that matched a recipe but the ones that matched a colour the workshop had learned to want.
prompt: [Academic — Ceramics] What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: The colour of this glaze is settled by the air reaching the fire rather than by the mixture put on the pot.

Uneven heat inside a kiln spoils more pieces than any other fault in the firing.
correct_answer: The colour of this glaze is settled by the air reaching the fire rather than by the mixture put on the pot.
explanation: The passage says at the outset that the colour depends less on the recipe than on the air in the kiln, and everything after that works out the consequence, which is the option about air reaching the fire rather than the mixture on the pot. Purity of ingredients is never mentioned; the closing sentence has the workshop keeping what matched a colour rather than a recipe, which reverses the option about judging by recipe; and the unevenness of a kiln load is one illustration rather than a ranking of faults.

passage:
A tontine was a way for a government to borrow without promising to repay the principal. Subscribers each paid in a sum and received a share of a fixed annual payment; when a subscriber died his share was divided among those still living, so that the income of every survivor rose. The last survivor drew the whole sum, and at his death the payments stopped and the debt was extinguished.

The arrangement suited a treasury because its outlay was known in advance and did not grow, whatever became of the number of subscribers. It suited a lender for a different reason: the return improved with age, at the point in life when other income was apt to be failing. What it did not do was price the loan accurately. A subscriber was free to nominate a life other than his own, and in the earliest schemes a subscription taken out on a healthy child cost no more than one taken out on its grandfather.
prompt: [Academic — Economic History] What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A form of state borrowing paid a fixed sum to a shrinking group of survivors and ended with the last of them.

A loan whose cost is fixed in advance is cheaper for a government than one whose cost follows the rate of interest.
correct_answer: A form of state borrowing paid a fixed sum to a shrinking group of survivors and ended with the last of them.
explanation: The first paragraph sets out a fixed annual payment divided among survivors and extinguished at the last death, and the second explains whom that suited, which is the option about a fixed sum paid to a shrinking group. The passage says a subscriber could nominate any life he chose rather than that treasuries sought young lenders; the attraction of income in old age is given as one reason among others and not as a ranking against safety; and rates of interest are never mentioned.

A qanat brings water from under a hillside to a village on the plain without a pump. A shaft is sunk until it reaches water-bearing gravel, and from its foot a tunnel is driven towards the village at a gradient much gentler than the slope of the ground above it. Because the tunnel falls away more slowly than the land does, it meets the surface some distance out on the plain, and the water runs out of its own accord.

The gradient is the whole difficulty. Too steep, and the current cuts into the floor of the tunnel and brings the roof down after it; too gentle, and the silt the water carries is left behind until the channel closes. A line of shafts along the route, sunk to lift out the spoil, is what remains visible of the work from above. They are kept open once the digging is over, because a tunnel that cannot be entered cannot be cleared.
prompt: [Academic — Hydraulic Engineering] According to the passage, the water reaches the surface out on the plain because
choices: the tunnel descends less steeply than the ground above it
the shafts along the route draw the water upward as it goes by
the gravel at the far end holds more water than the tunnel can carry
the tunnel is cut wider where it comes near the plain

A qanat brings water from under a hillside to a village on the plain without a pump. A shaft is sunk until it reaches water-bearing gravel, and from its foot a tunnel is driven towards the village at a gradient much gentler than the slope of the ground above it. Because the tunnel falls away more slowly than the land does, it meets the surface some distance out on the plain, and the water runs out of its own accord.

The gradient is the whole difficulty. Too steep, and the current cuts into the floor of the tunnel and brings the roof down after it; too gentle, and the silt the water carries is left behind until the channel closes. A line of shafts along the route, sunk to lift out the spoil, is what remains visible of the work from above. They are kept open once the digging is over, because a tunnel that cannot be entered cannot be cleared.

explanation: The remark is attached to the sentence about shafts being kept open once the digging is over and gives the reason for keeping them. The passage compares no costs; the gradient is justified separately by the need for the tunnel to meet the surface and by what happens when it is wrong; and how many shafts a route takes is never stated.

passage:
Spun yarn is not stable. Fibres are held together by the twist put into them, and that twist is always working to come out again; a length of single yarn hung free will kink back on itself until the turns are used up. The remedy is to ply two singles together in the direction opposite to the one they were spun in. The plying twist tightens as the twist of the singles unwinds, and the two come to rest against each other.

The direction is named for the slant the fibres take: a yarn spun clockwise slants like the middle stroke of the letter Z, one spun anticlockwise like the stroke of an S. A Z-spun single is therefore plied S. The convention matters to anyone repairing old cloth, because a thread plied the wrong way will not sit among its neighbours however carefully the colour has been matched.

correct_answer: turn back on itself until its twist is used up
explanation: The passage has single yarn kinking back on itself until the turns are used up, which is the option about turning back until the twist is used up. Slipping fibres are not described; holding its shape is the opposite of what the sentence reports; and the slant of an S names a direction of spinning rather than the behaviour of a hanging length.

passage:
In some tropical soils iron gathers in a layer a metre or so below the surface, carried there by a water table that rises and falls. While the layer stays wet it is soft enough to cut with a spade. Dug out and left in the sun, the same material hardens within weeks into a block that does not soften again when it is wetted. Buildings several centuries old stand on walls of it.

The change is not a matter of drying alone, since a sample kept damp in the dark loses water slowly and stays soft. What seems to be wanted is repeated wetting and drying at the surface, which draws the iron into a continuous framework through the clay. Once that framework has joined up the clay can no longer be worked, and land where the layer has been laid bare by erosion is lost to the plough.
prompt: [Academic — Soil Science] According to the passage, the layer can be cut with a spade as long as

correct_answer: it has not yet been dried out in the open
explanation: The passage keeps the layer soft until the material has been dug out and left in the sun to harden, which is the option about not yet having been dried out in the open. Iron washed further down would remove the layer rather than leave it soft; how the material is taken out is never made a condition of its softness; and the depth is given as a fact about where the layer sits, not as what keeps it workable.

passage:
Vitruvius describes bronze vessels set in niches under the seats of a Greek theatre, each tuned to a note of the scale and placed with its mouth opening towards the stage. His account is detailed: the vessels were to be arranged by interval across the width of the auditorium, and where bronze could not be afforded, jars of fired clay were to serve instead.

No theatre has been excavated with its vessels still in place. What survives at several sites is a row of empty niches of about the right size and position, and at a few of them the fittings that would have held something. Whether the vessels did what Vitruvius says they did is a separate question from whether they were there at all. A vessel tuned to one note takes up energy near that note and returns it a moment later, which would even out the loudness of a voice at some frequencies and might blur its consonants at others.

correct_answer: niches of about the size and position such vessels would need
explanation: What survives is described as a row of empty niches of about the right size and position, with fittings at a few of them, which is the option about niches of the size and position such vessels would need. No theatre has been excavated with its vessels in place; no record of cost is mentioned; and it is the vessels rather than the seating that Vitruvius has arranged by interval.
